abstract.p: 4-(Methylnitrosamino)-1-(3-pyridyl)-1-butanone (NNK) is a potent tobacco-specific nitrosamine that has been widely recognized as a major carcinogen contributing to smoking-related lung diseases. Although its involvement in lung cancer has been extensively studied, the underlying pathogenic mechanisms by which NNK contributes to the development of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) remain unclear.

In this study, potential IPF-related targets of NNK were identified through integrating multiple public databases. Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analyses were performed to uncover key biological processes associated with NNK-induced IPF. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) combined with machine learning approaches was employed to screen for core regulatory genes. Furthermore, molecular docking and 100-nanosecond molecular dynamics simulations were utilized to assess the binding interactions between NNK and candidate target proteins. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and immune infiltration analyses were also performed to validate gene expression patterns and characterize the immune microenvironment.

A total of 204 overlapping targets associated with both NNK exposure and IPF were identified, which were predominantly enriched in the biological processes of oxidative stress, cell cycle regulation, and the FoxO signaling pathway. Six hub genes (BCHE, CD38, MMP7, PLA2G2A, ST6GAL1, and TIMP1) were identified as potential key diagnostic biomarkers.

This study suggests that NNK may contribute to IPF progression through multiple mechanisms, including disrupting redox homeostasis, activating fibrotic signaling pathways, and modulating the immune microenvironment. The identified core genes and associated pathways provide novel insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying smoking-related IPF and offer promising targets for future therapeutic strategies.

sec.title: lntroduction
sec.p: 4-(Methylnitrosamino)-1-(3-pyridyl)-1-butanone (NNK) is recognized as the most potent carcinogenic aromatic compound among tobacco-specific nitrosamines (TSNAs) [1]. Its primary pathogenic mechanism is attributed to the electrophilic intermediates, such as α-hydroxylated derivatives of methyldiazohydroxide, which are directly generated through metabolism. These interact with DNA to form mutagenic adducts, including O⁶-methylguanine, ultimately leading to genomic instability [2]. Additionally, NNK activates α7-nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (α7-nAChR) and β-adrenergic receptors, initiating pro-inflammatory pathways (e.g., COX-2) and pro-fibrotic (such as E-cadherin downregulation-mediated EMT) pathways and oxidative stress signaling characterized by reactive oxygen species (ROS) bursts. This cascade of events impairs the immunosurveillance function of alveolar macrophages, as evidenced by the inhibition of IL-12 and TNF and the induction of IL-10, thereby collectively contributing to chronic lung tissue injury and remodeling [3, 4] Numerous studies have established that NNK plays a key role in the carcinogenesis associated with smoking-related lung cancer; however, its mechanisms in non-tumorous chronic lung diseases, particularly idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), remain inadequately explored. IPF is a fatal disease characterized by progressive fibrosis of the lung parenchyma for which no effective cure currently exists [5]. Actually, pulmonary fibrosis seriously endangers human health, with its incidence and mortality rates steadily increasing. The pathological mechanisms involve the initiation of persistent inflammation, abnormal activation of fibroblasts, and imbalance in extracellular matrix (ECM) metabolism. Despite this, the comprehensive molecular mechanisms implicated in pulmonary fibrosis pathogenesis remain largely unknown [6, 7]. Although its etiology remains elusive, research has identified a dose-dependent relationship between smoking exposure and an increased risk of developing IPF [8]. Furthermore, Mendelian randomization studies indicate that genetic susceptibility to smoking correlated with heightened risk of IPF, thereby providing evidence supporting a potential causal link between smoking and the pathogenesis of this disease [9]. Consequently, investigating the influence of key pathogenic factors related to smoking exposure, including NNK, on the development of IPF holds significant theoretical and practical implications.

NNK stands out as one of the representative strong carcinogens present in tobacco smoke and is predominantly found in mainstream smoke produced during active smoking. It is also widely present in environmental tobacco smoke (ETS) and secondhand smoke (SHS), which are inhaled passively, and has even been detected in thirdhand smoke (THS) [10, 11]. Although the concentration of nicotine in the air may diminish over time, NNK can continue to be generated hours after a tobacco product has been extinguished. This concealed and persistent presence exposes non-smokers to long-term risks that are often overlooked [12]. Given the prolonged exposure to NNK in tobacco smoke and its multifaceted impact on biological pathways—including immune regulation, fibrosis, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation—NNK not only harms smokers but may also cause lasting damage in high-risk populations intermittently exposed to low doses, such as children, the elderly, and individuals with chronic lung diseases [13].

Notably, the toxicological consequences of NNK extend beyond lung cancer; it may significantly contribute to the pathogenesis of chronic lung conditions like idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Current gene therapies for chronic lung diseases aim to regulate hereditary gene mutations or acquired gene deregulations, yet developing effective delivery vectors remains a major challenge. Therefore, it is crucial to investigate changes in the major genes expressed in the lungs during pathological states to identify genetic targets for the development of effective treatments [14, 15]. Therefore, conducting comprehensive research into the network toxicological effects of NNK within the context of IPF pathogenesis is essential for uncovering its potential pathogenic mechanisms and providing a theoretical foundation for developing effective public health intervention strategies.

Network toxicology serves as a systematic research tool capable of elucidating the multi-level biological effects induced by chemicals within a biological system. It is particularly adept at clarifying how NNK contributes to the pathogenesis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) [16]. This approach integrates multi-omics data alongside signaling pathway analysis, thereby facilitating an understanding of how NNK disrupts cellular functions, gene expression patterns, and signaling transduction networks. Furthermore, through molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulation techniques, one can predict binding modes and structural stability changes between NNK and key biological targets more accurately. Through this multidimensional and interdisciplinary approach, it is anticipated that the crucial role of NNK in the pathogenesis of IPF will be elucidated comprehensively, thereby providing a robust theoretical foundation for its toxicological risk assessment and prevention measures.

sec.title: Collection of NNK targets
sec.p: We retrieved the chemical structure and Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) notation of NNK from the PubChem database (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/). Potential NNK targets were identified using the CTD, STITCH, Swiss Target Prediction, PharmMapper, SEA, and Galaxyweb databases, with the species specified as “Homo sapiens.” After merging the targets and removing duplicates, we generated a comprehensive list of NNK-related target genes.

sec.title: Acquisition of disease targets for Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF)
sec.p: We obtained disease target genes for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) by searching the GeneCards database (with a score > 1), TTD, and OMIM using the keyword “idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.” After merging the targets from each dataset and removing duplicates, we created a comprehensive list of IPF-related disease target genes.

sec.title: Functional pathway analysis and PPI analysis of target genes
sec.p: We performed Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses using the MSigDB database to explore the molecular pathways involved in NNK-induced IPF. Our analysis covered three GO domains (biological process, cellular component, and molecular function) and KEGG pathways to gain insights into the biological functions and molecular mechanisms of the identified genes. Significantly enriched pathways were determined based on an adjusted p-value < 0.05. We used the STRING database to examine protein-protein interactions (PPI) among the genes, with a confidence score threshold of ≥ 0.7. Isolated nodes were removed to retain biologically relevant interactions. The generated PPI network was visualized using Cytoscape 3.10.3.

sec.title: GEO data acquisition
sec.p: A total of six transcriptomic datasets were retrieved from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/). GSE47460 was utilized as the discovery cohort, comprising 582 subjects, including 254 patients with interstitial lung disease (ILD), 220 with COPD, and 108 healthy controls. Two datasets, GSE150910 (82 cHP, 103 IPF, and 103 controls) and GSE213001 (20 IPF, 9 non-IPF ILD, and 14 controls), were employed for internal consistency assessment. To evaluate the model’s generalizability, we incorporated GSE32537 (167 IIP and 50 controls) and GSE53845 (40 IPF and 8 controls) as independent external cohorts.Single-cell Dataset: For cell-type specific analysis, the scRNA-seq dataset GSE122960 was included, featuring lung tissue samples from 8 fibrosis patients and 8 transplant donors.

sec.title: Identification of core genes using WGCNA
sec.p: After integrating the RNA-seq data downloaded from the GEO database, sample clustering was performed to identify and exclude outlier samples to ensure the quality of the samples for subsequent analyses. The key steps included processing the trait data corresponding to IPF patients and healthy controls to facilitate the analysis of module-trait relationships. The optimal soft threshold (β = 0.9) was determined using the “pickSoftThreshold” function in the WGCNA package, which is crucial for constructing the weighted gene co-expression network. Based on this optimal threshold, adjacency and topological overlap matrices (TOM) similarity matrices were constructed. Gene co-expression modules were identified using the dynamic tree cutting method. Finally, the correlation between module eigengenes and traits, the membership of each gene within modules, and the significance of genes to the traits were quantified.

sec.title: Integration and batch effect correction
sec.p: To facilitate a robust cross-dataset analysis, data integration was performed to minimize potential batch effects stemming from diverse sequencing platforms, chronological variations, and disparate laboratory conditions. Specifically, the “sva” R package was employed to harmonize the expression profiles. We utilized the ComBat function, which implements a parametric empirical Bayesian framework, to adjust for known batch-related technical variations. This process ensured that the biological signals were preserved while the systematic noise across the integrated cohorts was effectively eliminated.

sec.title: Machine learning-based diagnostic model construction
sec.p: A machine learning approach was developed to construct a diagnostic model for IPF patients. The model was trained and evaluated using one training set and three validation sets. Algorithms such as Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), Random Forest (RF), Ridge Regression, Elastic Net Regression (Enet), Lasso, Gradient Boosting Machine (GBM), Naive Bayes, Partial Least Squares Regression (plsRglm), and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) were employed. Each algorithm was optimized using ten-fold cross-validation, and parameters were adjusted to enhance the model’s adaptability and accuracy. The performance of the models was assessed using Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves, and confusion matrices were constructed to validate the model’s practical utility in distinguishing IPF patients from healthy individuals.

sec.title: SHAP model interpretation
sec.p: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis was used to evaluate the best-performing model, elucidate its prediction mechanism, and quantify the contribution and relative importance of each feature to the prediction outcome. This interpretable method provided a rigorous insight into the model’s decision-making process.

sec.title: Immune cell infiltration analysis
sec.p: Single-sample Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (ssGSEA) was performed using the GSVA R package (v1.46.0) to carefully examine the infiltration scores of immune-related cells between IPF lesions and normal tissues. Statistical significance was assessed using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test, and the correlation between core target genes and immune cell infiltration was analyzed.

sec.title: Functional exploration of hubs via ssGSEA
sec.p: To investigate the biological impact of core genes on IPF pathogenesis, samples were divided into high- and low-expression groups based on the median expression levels of the most strongly correlated genes. Pathway activity scores were calculated using ssGSEA with the “GSVA” package (v1.48.3) and signature gene sets from the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB, v7.5.1). Differential pathway activities between groups were analyzed to identify mechanisms linking the core genes to IPF progression.

sec.title: Single-cell sequencing analysis
sec.p: Single-cell RNA sequencing data from the GSE122960 dataset were comprehensively preprocessed and annotated, followed by visualization. The results showed that core genes were differentially expressed in various cell types.

sec.title: Molecular docking technology
sec.p: Molecular docking was performed to evaluate the binding activity of NNK with target proteins. The PDB database (https://www.rcsb.org/) was used to retrieve and download the PDB files and 2D structure files of key target proteins. The 3D structure of NNK was obtained from the PubChem database (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/). Docking simulations were conducted using the CB-Dock2 platform (https://cadd.labshare.cn/cb-dock2/index.php). Binding activity was assessed based on the binding sites and binding energies between NNK and target proteins. A binding energy equal to or less than − 5.0 kcal/mol was considered indicative of satisfactory target binding activity.

sec.title: Molecular dynamics simulation
sec.p: Molecular dynamics simulations of the complex system were carried out for 100 nanoseconds using Gromacs 2022 software. The protein force field employed was Charmm36, while the ligand force field was GAFF. Solvent was added to the protein-ligand system using the TIP3P water model, and a water box with periodic boundary conditions of 1.0 nm was constructed. The Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) method and Verlet algorithm were used to handle electrostatic interactions. Subsequently, equilibration simulations were performed in the isothermal-isochoric (NVT) ensemble and isothermal-isobaric (NPT) ensemble for 1 million steps each. Finally, the simulation was completed for a total of 100 nanoseconds under constant temperature (300 K) and constant pressure (1 bar) conditions using Gromacs 2022.

sec.title: Animal model of IPF
sec.p: All animal experiments were approved by the Ethics Committee of Xiangya Hospital, Central South University (NO.202406127). Pulmonary fibrosis was induced in four-week-old C57BL/6 mice via a single intratracheal (i.t.) injection of bleomycin (BLM, 5 mg/kg) under anesthesia. To specifically investigate the role of NNK in the progression of fibrosis rather than the initial acute inflammatory response, NNK administration was initiated on Day 9 post-BLM induction. This time point was selected based on established models indicating that the transition from acute inflammation to active fibrogenesis occurs around Day 7–9 [17, 18]. From Day 9, mice received intraperitoneal (i.p.) injections of NNK (50 or 100 mg/kg) every 2 days. The mice were maintained under controlled environmental conditions and were sacrificed on Day 21 for subsequent analysis.

sec.title: Western blotting
sec.p: Proteins from liver tissues and cells were washed three times with cold 1× PBS and extracted using 1× RIPA buffer (Thermo, Waltham, MA, USA) supplemented with a protease inhibitor cocktail. Protein concentrations were determined using the BCA Protein Assay Kit (Yeasen Biotechnology (Shanghai) Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). Equal amounts of protein (20–40 µg per sample) were subjected to SDS-PAGE (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA) and transferred onto polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes (Bio-Rad). After blocking with 5% non-fat milk for 1 h, the membranes were incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies. The membranes were then incubated with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibodies for 1 h at room temperature. Protein bands were visualized using chemiluminescence on a IMAGEQUANT800.

sec.title: Real-time fluorescence quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR)
sec.p: Total RNA was isolated from cells using Trizol reagent (TAKARA, Shiga, Japan), followed by cDNA synthesis with HiScript III RT SuperMix (Vazyme, Nanjing, China). Quantitative real-time PCR was performed with ChamQ Universal SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme). Gene expression levels were calculated using the 2−ΔΔCT method, and the mRNA levels were normalized to the control group, which was assigned a value of 1. MMP7, Forward primer: ATGTGGAGTGCCAGATGTTGC. Reverse primer: AGCAGTTCCCCATACAACTTTC. BCHE, Forward primer: GTCAGAGGGATGAACTTGACAG, Reverse primer: TGAATCGAAGTCTACCAAGAGGT. CD38, Forward primer: CAACTCTGTCTTGGCGTCAGT, Reverse primer: CCCATACACTTTGGCAGTCTACA. PLA2G2A, Forward primer: ATGAAGACCCTCCTACTGTTGG, Reverse primer: GCTTCCTTTCCTGTCGTCAACT. ST6GAL1, Forward primer: AACTCTCAGTTGGTTACCACAGA, Reverse primer: GGTGCAGCTTACGATAAGTCTT. TIMP1-F, Forward primer: CTTCTGCAATTCCGACCTCGT, Reverse primer: ACGCTGGTATAAGGTGGTCTG.

sec.title: Antibodies and reagents
sec.p: NNK was obtained from Macklin. Antibodies used were as follows: MMP7 (ET1702-50, ZENBIO, Chengdu, China), α-SMA (19245 S, Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA), COL1A1 (72026 S, Cell Signaling Technology, 67288-1-Ig, proteintech), GAPDH(60004-1-Ig, proteintech). Human MMP7 Elisa kit(BN0096-HB, BAINIAN SHENGWU). Methyllycaconitine citrate(HY-N2332A, MCE).

sec.title: Cell culture
sec.p: The human MRC-5cell line was sourced from Procell Life Science (Wuhan, China). Cells were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) (Gibco, MA, USA, 11965092), supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, NEWZERUM, Christchurch, New Zealand) and 1% antibiotic solution (Coolaber, Beijing, China). Cultures were incubated at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 atmosphere. The cell line was authenticated via short tandem repeat (STR) profiling, and testing confirmed the absence of mycoplasma contamination. MRC-5 cells were seeded and allowed to adhere overnight. To simulate environmental exposure, cells were incubated with NNK at biologically relevant concentrations (1 and 10 ng/mL) for 48 h. For receptor blocking assays, cells were pre-treated with the specific α7-nAChR antagonist MLA (100 nM) for 1 h, followed by co-incubation with NNK (10 ng/mL) for an additional 48 h. Cells treated with the vehicle served as controls.

sec.title: Purpose of AI use
sec.p: No generative AI was used in the research and manuscript development, with the exception of utilizing DeepSeek solely for text polishing purposes. This statement is hereby declared [19].

sec.title: Screening and functional annotation of potential NNK-IPF targets
sec.p: To identify the targets of NNK-IPF, we screened 37 target genes from the TTD database using “idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis” as the keyword, 99 target genes from the OMIM database, and 5,596 target genes from GeneCards (with a score > 1). By integrating these three databases, a total of 5,631 IPF target genes were determined (Fig. 1A). After searching six databases—CTD, STITCH, Swiss Target Prediction, Pharmmapper, SEA, and Galaxyweb—with the species specified as “Homo sapiens” and removing duplicates, we identified 326 target genes for NNK (Fig. 1B). The intersection of the 326 NNK targets and the 5,631 IPF targets yielded 204 common NNK-IPF targets (Fig. 1C).

caption.p: Identification and analysis of intersecting targets related to NNK and disease. A Venn diagram showing the overlapping targets of NNK identified across three different databases. B Venn diagram of disease-related targets obtained from six databases. C Intersection of NNK-related targets and disease-related targets, indicating potential shared targets. D KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of the intersecting targets between NNK and the disease. E Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of the intersecting targets, including biological process, cellular component, and molecular function categories. F Protein-protein interaction (PPI) network constructed from the intersecting targets, illustrating potential functional interactions

sec.p: To further explore the biological functions of the potential target genes of NNK in the induction of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and the signaling pathways they are involved in, we conducted Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses on the intersecting genes. The GO analysis covered three functional categories: biological process (BP), cellular component (CC), and molecular function (MF). We selected the top 5 most significant entries in each category to create bar charts, as shown in Fig. 1D and E. In the BP category, the intersecting genes were significantly enriched in terms such as “response to xenobiotic stimulus,” “rhythmic process,” “response to oxidative stress,” and “response to decreased oxygen levels.” In the CC category, the target genes were mainly enriched in domains such as “protein kinase complex” and “transferase complex.” In the MF category, the enriched terms included “protein serine/threonine kinase activity” and “histone modifier enzyme activity.” KEGG pathway analysis further revealed that the intersecting genes are involved in multiple signaling pathways closely related to diseases, including “chemical carcinogenesis—receptor activation,” “FoxO signaling pathway,” “cell cycle,” and “apoptosis” (Fig. 1E).

We imported the NNK-IPF-related targets into the STRING database and screened the top-ranked targets with a confidence score of ≥ 0.7. These target data were then imported into Cytoscape software for network construction. The results are shown in Fig. 1F, where darker colors and larger circle sizes indicating stronger protein-protein interactions.

sec.title: Construction of a co-expression network and identification of key module genes
sec.p: To minimize batch effects as much as possible, we integrated three datasets—GSE47460, GSE150910, and GSE2130001—and performed comprehensive normalization on the combined gene expression matrix. Principal component analysis (PCA) before normalization revealed significant batch bias among samples; however, after normalization, PCA results showed marked improvement in sample distribution, with tighter and more consistent clustering across different datasets, indicating effective correction of batch effects and better reflection of underlying biological differences (Fig. 2A–B). Based on the normalized expression matrix, we applied the WGCNA method to construct a weighted gene co-expression network. First, we used the “pickSoftThreshold” function to select the optimal soft threshold to ensure the construction of a scale-free network. Results indicated that when the soft threshold was β = 5, the network achieved a high degree of fit while maintaining a reasonable average connectivity (Fig. 2C). On this basis, we constructed the adjacency matrix and topological overlap matrix (TOM) and used hierarchical clustering and dynamic tree cutting methods to cluster genes. Ultimately, co-expression modules were identified, with strong independence between modules (Fig. 2D). Module-trait relationship analysis showed that red and turquoise co-expression modules were significantly associated with IPF, suggesting that these modules may play important roles in disease development (Fig. 2E). By integrating the NNK-IPF genes from conventional analysis with the module genes from WGCNA (after removing duplicates), we determined a final set of 20 relevant genes (Fig. 2F).

caption.p: WGCNA Analysis in the Training Set. A Principal component analysis (PCA) plot before batch effect integration. This panel illustrates the initial distribution of samples in the training set, highlighting potential batch effects or confounding factors. B PCA plot after batch effect correction. The corrected PCA plot demonstrates the improved clustering of samples, indicating successful removal of batch effects and better representation of biological variation. C Selection of the optimal soft-threshold power for weighted gene co-expression network analysis. This plot shows the scale-free topology fit index and mean connectivity for various soft-threshold powers, with the optimal power chosen to ensure a scale-free network. D Hierarchical clustering dendrograms of genes and clinical traits in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). The dendrograms display the hierarchical clustering of genes and clinical traits, revealing the organization of gene expression patterns and their association with clinical phenotypes. E Module-trait correlation heatmap of co-expression modules in IPF. This heatmap shows the correlation coefficients and p -values between gene co-expression modules and clinical traits, highlighting the most significant associations. F Venn diagram depicting overlaps between target genes and hub genes in the WGCNA-derived red and turquoise modules. This diagram illustrates the intersection of genes identified as hubs in the co-expression network and those of interest in the study, providing insights into key regulatory genes in IPF

sec.title: Machine learning-based screening and validation of core diagnostic biomarkers
sec.p: Through comprehensive machine learning analysis of the 20 candidate targets, we constructed a predictive model to identify core genes involved in NNK-related IPF. The LASSO-RF combined model performed the best across all datasets(supplementary 1), demonstrating stable and excellent predictive ability (Fig. 3A). The model’s discrimination performance was further assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and confusion matrices (Figs. 3B–I). In the training set GSE47460, the LASSO-RF model achieved an AUC value of 0.996 (95% CI: 0.991–0.999), and in the validation sets GSE213001, GSE150910, and GSE32537, the AUC values were 0.992, 0.852, and 0.969, respectively, all showing strong generalization and diagnostic performance (Figs. 3B–E). Confusion matrices further validated the model’s classification accuracy, with particularly high sensitivity and specificity in GSE213001 and GSE32537 (Figs. 3F–I).

caption.p: Development and validation of the IPF diagnostic model. A Construction of diagnostic features using various machine learning algorithms individually or in combination. The performance of these features was evaluated by their AUC values in the training set (GSE47460) and validation sets (GSE150910, GSE213001, GSE32537). The diagnostic feature built using the LASSO-RF algorithm demonstrated superior performance. B-I Validation of the LASSO-RF diagnostic feature: (B, C, D, E) AUC curves in datasets GSE47460, GSE213001, GSE150910, and GSE32537, respectively. F, G, H, I Confusion matrices in datasets GSE47460, GSE213001, GSE150910, and GSE32537, respectively

sec.title: Validation and clinical application of the core gene signature
sec.p: To further validate the expression levels of the core genes identified by the LASSO-RF model, we assessed their expression differences in an external dataset, GSE53845 (Figs. 4A–F). The results showed that BCHE (Fig. 4A) was significantly upregulated in the IPF group (P < 0.001); CD38 (Fig. 4B) exhibited significantly elevated expression (P < 0.001); MMP7 (Fig. 4C), a known IPF biomarker, had significantly higher expression levels compared to the normal group (P < 0.001); PLA2G2A (Fig. 4D) was also significantly upregulated in IPF (P < 0.01); ST6GAL1 (Fig. 4E) showed significant differences (P < 0.001), suggesting its potential regulatory role in the disease state; and TIMP1 (Fig. 4F) was significantly upregulated in IPF patients (P < 0.05). To further dissect the internal decision-making mechanism of the model, we performed SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) interpretability analysis on the LASSO-RF model. The SHAP bar plot revealed that MMP7 had the highest average SHAP value (0.177) among all model genes, making it the most critical feature influencing model predictions, followed by BCHE (0.067), ST6GAL1 (0.061), CD38 (0.052), PLA2G2A (0.052), and TIMP1 (0.043) (Fig. 5A). As shown in Fig. 5B, high expression levels of MMP7 and BCHE were significantly associated with a positive increase in the predicted IPF values. ST6GAL1 and TIMP1 exhibited bidirectional regulatory effects. Based on these six key feature genes, we constructed a nomogram model for the diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) (Fig. 5C), which can provide personalized disease risk prediction scores for each individual. The calibration curve demonstrated good consistency between the actual and predicted probabilities of the nomogram, indicating high accuracy of the model in clinical applications (Fig. 5D). Additionally, decision curve analysis (DCA) results showed that the model achieved high net benefits across the majority of threshold probability intervals, suggesting its potential value in clinical decision-making (Fig. 5E).

sec.title: Analysis of the immune microenvironment and functional pathways of core genes
sec.p: To further elucidate the immune microenvironment characteristics of IPF, we employed single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) to quantitatively assess the relative abundance of immune cells. The results showed that the infiltration levels of several immune cell subsets were significantly altered in IPF patient tissues (Fig. 6A). Compared with normal tissues, the infiltration levels of activated B cells, CD4⁺ T cells, and memory B cells were significantly increased in IPF tissues, while the infiltration levels of eosinophils and neutrophils were significantly decreased. Further analysis of the correlation between model genes and immune cell infiltration (Fig. 6B) revealed that genes such as MMP7 were significantly positively correlated with activated B cells and CD56^bright natural killer cells but negatively correlated with eosinophils and Th17 cells. Overall, the six core model genes showed consistent correlation trends across various immune cell types. To explore the potential functions of the core genes in IPF, we divided the samples into high and low expression groups based on their median expression levels and performed enrichment analysis using ssGSEA combined with MSigDB hallmark gene sets. The results showed significant heterogeneity in the pathways associated with different genes, suggesting that they may play complementary or synergistic roles in IPF. Specifically, BCHE was enriched in immune pathways such as “inflammatory response” and “IFNγ response” (Fig. 7A); CD38 was associated with “graft-versus-host disease” and “cell cycle checkpoints” (Fig. 7B); MMP7 was involved in “interferon response” and “TNFα signaling” (Fig. 7C); PLA2G2A was related to “EMT” and “hypoxia response” (Fig. 7D); ST6GAL1 was enriched in “interferon response” and “K-Ras inhibition” (Fig. 7E); and TIMP1 activated pathways such as “E2F targets” and “G2M checkpoint” (Fig. 7F).

caption.p: Immune Infiltration Analysis in IPF. A Single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) of immune infiltration in IPF. The relative abundance of various immune cells in IPF samples was assessed using ssGSEA, revealing distinct immune cell infiltration profiles. B Correlation between model genes and immune cells. The expression levels of model genes were analyzed for their correlations with different immune cell types, providing insights into the potential interactions between gene expression and immune cell infiltration in IPF

Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) Results. A-F Pathway enrichment results for model genes in the KEGG database. Each panel represents a different pathway enriched by the model genes, with the enrichment score (ES) indicating the degree of gene set enrichment. The normalized enrichment score (NES) and false discovery rate (FDR) q-values are provided to assess the significance of each pathway. The red and blue portions of the enrichment plot correspond to genes that are highly expressed in the experimental and control groups, respectively

sec.title: Single-cell RNA-Seq analysis reveals cellular localization of core genes
sec.p: To validate the expression profiles of the core genes at the cellular level, we analyzed the single-cell RNA-seq dataset GSE122960. First, we performed quality control and filtering on the raw data (Fig. 8A) and identified various cell types based on characteristic cell markers, including monocytes/macrophages, epithelial cells, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, T/NK cells, B cells, plasma cells, and mast cells (Figs. 8B, C). We also validated the expression patterns of the six model genes (BCHE, CD38, MMP7, PLA2G2A, ST6GAL1, and TIMP1) at the single-cell level, and the results showed differential expression across various cell subtypes. For example, TIMP1 was significantly expressed in monocytes/macrophages and fibroblasts, while MMP7 was mainly enriched in epithelial cells (Fig. 8D).

caption.p: Single-Cell Sequencing Results. A Data filtering process of the single-cell sequencing dataset. The workflow illustrates the steps taken to filter out low-quality cells and noise, ensuring the reliability of downstream analyses. B t-SNE plot of 11 cell types. Cells are colored according to their annotated cell types, revealing distinct clusters representing different cellular populations within the dataset C Expression levels of the top three marker genes identified by FindAllMarkers in each cell type. The plot displays the distribution and abundance of these marker genes across various cell types, highlighting their differential expression patterns. D Validation of model genes in the single-cell dataset. The expression of model genes is assessed across different cell types to confirm their relevance and consistency in the context of single-cell analysis

sec.title: Molecular docking analysis of NNK binding interactions with proteins
sec.p: To verify the potential binding interactions between NNK and the proteins encoded by the core genes (BCHE, CD38, MMP7, PLA2G2A, ST6GAL1, and TIMP1) that we had previously identified, we conducted systematic molecular docking analyses. The results showed that the binding energies of NNK with all six target proteins were lower than − 5 kcal/mol (see Supplementary 2), indicating that these interactions are highly stable and thermodynamically spontaneous. Further visualization of the docking conformations of the complexes (Fig. 9) revealed that all AFB1-protein complexes formed stable docking structures, supporting their potential biological interactions.

caption.p: Conformational Analysis of Molecular Docking between Model Genes and NNK The potential binding conformations between NNK and the proteins encoded by the core genes (A) BCHE, (B) CD38, (C) MMP7, (D) PLA2G2A, (E) ST6GAL1, and (F) TIMP1 were analyzed. The results demonstrate that NNK forms stable complexes with all six target proteins, with binding energies lower than −5 kcal/mol, indicating highly stable and thermodynamically spontaneous interactions

sec.title: Molecular dynamics simulations confirm stable binding of NNK to core targets
sec.p: Since the complexes of BCHE, CD38, ST6GAL1, and TIMP1 exhibited significant conformational fluctuations or lower stability in molecular dynamics simulations, this study focuses on presenting detailed analytical results for the MMP7-NNK and PLA2G2A-NNK complexes. Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the PLA2G2A–NNK complex rapidly reached equilibrium within 20 ns, with RMSD fluctuations of approximately 0.5 nm, while the MMP7–NNK complex required 50 ns to reach equilibrium but demonstrated smaller fluctuations (around 0.2 nm) (Fig. 10A and D). The radius of gyration (Rg) of both complexes remained stable throughout the simulation(Fig. 10B and E), and the solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) was maintained within a reasonable range (Fig. 10C and F). Hydrogen bond analysis indicated that both the MMP7–NNK and PLA2G2A–NNK complexes consistently formed approximately two hydrogen bonds (Fig. 10G and I). Root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) analysis showed that most residues exhibited fluctuations below 0.3 nm (Fig. 10H and J), confirming low structural flexibility and high conformational stability in these two complexes. Overall, the results demonstrate that MMP7 and PLA2G2A form stable interactions with NNK and exhibit significant binding potential.

caption.p: Molecular Dynamics Simulations of Protein-Ligand Complexes. (A, D)​ Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD) of the PLA2G2A–NNK and MMP7–NNK complexes over time, respectively. RMSD measures the average distance between the atoms of the simulated structure and the reference structure, indicating the stability of the complexes.(B, E)​ Radius of Gyration (Rg) of the PLA2G2A–NNK and MMP7–NNK complexes over time, respectively. Rg reflects the compactness of the protein structure.(C, F)​ Solvent-Accessible Surface Area (SASA) of the PLA2G2A–NNK and MMP7–NNK complexes over time, respectively. SASA indicates the surface area of the protein accessible to solvent molecules.(G, I)​ Hydrogen bond (H-bond) analysis of the PLA2G2A–NNK and MMP7–NNK complexes over time, respectively. The number of hydrogen bonds formed between the protein and ligand is plotted.(H, J)​ Root Mean Square Fluctuation (RMSF) of backbone atoms for the PLA2G2A–NNK and MMP7–NNK complexes, respectively. RMSF measures the flexibility of individual residues, revealing regions of the protein that undergo significant conformational changes during the simulation

sec.title: NNK exacerbates BLM-induced pulmonary fibrosis via MMP7 upregulation
sec.p: In MRC-5 cells, NNK treatment (48 h) dose-dependently upregulated MMP7 mRNA and protein levels, as well as the fibrotic markers COL1A1 and α-SMA (Fig. 11A, B). Concurrently, qPCR analysis revealed a significant dose-dependent upregulation of other hub genes, including TIMP1, CD38, and PLA2G2A, accompanied by a marked downregulation of BCHE (Fig. 11A). ELISA confirmed increased MMP7 secretion in supernatants (Fig. 11C). To verify the involvement of the predicted receptor, cells were co-treated with the α7-nAChR antagonist Methyllycaconitine (MLA). Crucially, MLA attenuated the NNK-induced upregulation of MMP7, COL1A1, and α-SMA (Fig. 11D), suggesting that this pro-fibrotic response may be dependent on α7-nAChR signaling. In vivo, C57BL/6 mice were administered Bleomycin (BLM, i.t.) followed by NNK treatment (i.p.) every two days (Fig. 11E). Compared to the BLM + PBS group, NNK administration (50 and 100 mg/kg) significantly aggravated lung inflammation and structural damage. Furthermore, NNK treatment increased collagen deposition and MMP7 expression in lung tissues, as evidenced by Masson’s trichrome and immunohistochemical staining, respectively (Fig. 11F).

Cells were treated with the indicated concentrations of NNK (0, 1, 10 ng/ml) for 48 hours. A Relative mRNA expression levels were determined by RT-qPCR (n = [3]). B Protein levels of COL1A1, α-SMA, and MMP7 were measured by Western blot. β-actin was used as a loading control. C The secretion of MMP7 in the cell culture supernatant was detected by ELISA (n = [3]). D Immunoblot analysis of COL1A1, α-SMA, and MMP7 in MRC-5 cells following stimulation with NNK (10 ng/ml) with or without MLA (100 nM) co-treatment. The "+" and "-" signs indicate the presence or absence of the respective compounds. β-actin serves as the loading control. E Schematic diagram of the experimental protocol. C57BL/6 mice were intratracheally (i.t.) administered with Bleomycin (BLM, 5 mg/kg) on day 0. Starting from day 9, mice received intraperitoneal (i.p.) injections of NNK (50 or 100 mg/kg) every 2 days until sacrifice on day 21. F Representative images of lung tissue sections from each group. Left panel: H&E staining showing lung inflammation and structural damage. Middle panel: Masson’s trichrome staining indicating collagen deposition (blue). Right panel: Immunohistochemical staining for MMP7 distribution. Original magnification: ×200 (20× objective). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ****P < 0.0001 vs. control group (0 ng/ml) or BLM+PBS group

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a highly heterogeneous interstitial lung disease characterized by a poor prognosis. Despite its relatively low global prevalence, IPF is associated with a high mortality rate. Current therapeutic options, such as pirfenidone and nintedanib, are limited to slowing disease progression and do not reverse the underlying pathological changes [20–22]. Therefore, gaining a deeper insight into the molecular mechanisms driven by environmental exposures is essential to pave the way for identifying new therapeutic targets.

Epidemiological data indicate that smoking is one of the most well-established environmental risk factors for IPF, with over 60% of patients having a history of smoking [8, 23]. Multiple carcinogens present in cigarette smoke are believed to contribute to alveolar epithelial cell injury, fibroblast activation, and disruption of immune homeostasis [24]. Among these carcinogens is the tobacco-specific nitrosamine NNK, which is a significant carcinogen produced during nicotine metabolism. NNK has been shown to induce chronic inflammation and fibrotic changes in lung tissue following long-term exposure [25]. Although NNK has been extensively studied as a promoter of lung cancer, its network toxicological mechanisms in the development of IPF have yet to be fully elucidated.

This study explores the potential pathogenic mechanisms of NNK in IPF from a systems biology perspective. The convergence of multiple databases suggests that NNK disrupts lung tissue homeostasis and fibrotic processes by inducing oxidative stress, interfering with the cell cycle, and activating the FoxO pathway. Through the integration of expression networks and the development of machine learning models, six key genes—BCHE, CD38, MMP7, PLA2G2A, ST6GAL1, and TIMP1—were identified; all exhibited strong predictive performance and clinical discrimination. Immune infiltration analysis indicates that these genes may play a role in remodeling the immune microenvironment by influencing the infiltration of immune cells such as B cells and T cells, thereby accelerating IPF progression.

Among them, the gene MMP7 stands out for its pivotal role in IPF. Numerous studies have confirmed its significantly elevated expression levels in plasma from IPF patients as well as in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) and lung tissues; this elevation is closely associated with disease severity [26]. MMP7 is primarily expressed by lung epithelial cells, macrophages, and fibroblasts. It facilitates fibroblast proliferation and extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling during fibrosis through mechanisms such as cleaving E-cadherin or activating pro-HB-EGF [27, 28]. Additionally, polymorphisms within its promoter region may enhance transcription activity, potentially exacerbating disease progression [29]. Consequently, MMP7 not only holds promise as a biomarker for diagnosing and classifying IPF but also serves as an important downstream effector of NNK-mediated fibrotic effects.

Single-cell analysis has elucidated the specific expression of the aforementioned core genes in epithelial cells, fibroblasts, and immune cells, thereby supporting their potential regulatory functions across different cell populations. Molecular docking and dynamics simulation results further indicated that NNK can stably bind to multiple target proteins, exhibiting higher conformational stability, particularly in MMP7, ST6GAL1, and PLA2G2A. This suggests potential direct regulatory capabilities. However, we acknowledge that these specific interactions are currently supported primarily by computational predictions; the lack of direct biophysical validation (e.g., Surface Plasmon Resonance) for binding kinetics remains a limitation of this study and will be a priority in our future investigations.

Notably, our in vitro and in vivo experiments provided robust validation for these bioinformatic predictions. We observed that NNK exposure dose-dependently upregulated MMP7 expression in MRC-5 fibroblasts and aggravated pulmonary fibrosis in Bleomycin-treated mice, confirming MMP7 as a critical functional effector in NNK-mediated pathology. Collectively, these findings imply that NNK may intervene in the development of IPF through various pathways and targets, encompassing critical aspects such as oxidative stress, immune imbalance, and disruption of the cell cycle. This provides theoretical support for understanding the pathological mechanisms underlying smoking-related IPF while expanding the research direction for potential intervention strategies.

In IPF, it is essential to precisely regulate the expression patterns of protein kinases, fibrosis-promoting factors, and genes involved in inflammatory responses -especially within alveolar epithelial cells, fibroblasts, and immune cells. As a potent electrophile and stimulator of signaling pathways [30], NNK not only reinforces fibrotic pathways through α7 nAChR activation, β-adrenergic receptors, inflammatory feedback, and ROS generation but may also influence RNA stability of key signaling molecules by interfering with METTL14/YTHDF2-mediated m6A modification [31, 32]. For example, RNA modification can modulate the expression dynamics of pathways such as E2F, TGF-β, FoxO, and NF-κB within fibroblasts, thereby impacting the IPF phenotype. Future research could further investigate how NNK affects the m6A modification network and explore whether it promotes pulmonary tissue fibrosis through epigenetic mechanisms [33, 34].

Additionally, in neuroendocrine lung tumor models, such as small cell lung cancer (SCLC), NNK has been shown to promote cellular proliferation by activating the Raf-1/ERK1/2/c-Myc/Bcl-2 signaling axis. This pathway may also contribute to the neuro-immuno-fibrotic crosstalk observed in IPF. The NNK-induced overexpression of α7 nAChR, combined with hypoxia adaptation responses -such as serotonin-mediated activation of the PKC–Raf–ERK pathway -can further enhance epithelial-mesenchymal transition and fibroblast activity, thereby driving the relentless progression of fibrosis.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a fatal disease strongly associated with cigarette smoking, yet the specific fibrotic mechanisms of the tobacco-specific nitrosamine NNK have remained elusive. In this study, we combined systems biology predictions with robust in vitro and in vivo validation to demonstrate that NNK significantly exacerbates pulmonary fibrosis by upregulating MMP7. We observed that NNK exposure dose-dependently increased MMP7 expression in human lung fibroblasts and aggravated tissue remodeling in bleomycin-treated mice, confirming MMP7 as a critical downstream effector. Crucially, our receptor blocking experiments confirmed that this pro-fibrotic response is mediated through the α7-nAChR signaling pathway. While MMP7 is known to drive fibrosis via ECM degradation and pro-fibrotic activation, the precise signaling axis linking NNK receptor binding (e.g., to α7-nAChR) to MMP7 transcriptional activation remains to be fully elucidated. It is plausible that NNK triggers downstream kinase cascades, such as MAPK or PI3K/Akt, to recruit transcription factors to the MMP7 promoter. Future investigations should prioritize dissecting these intracellular pathways to identify druggable targets that can interrupt this environmental toxin-driven fibrotic progression.
